source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει· καί ποτε προαγαγεῖν βουληθεὶς αὐτοὺς περὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων εἰς λόγους τῶν τῇδε τῇ πόλει τὰ ἀρχαιότατα λέγειν ἐπιχειρεῖ, περὶ Φορωνέως τε τοῦ πρώτου λεχθέντος καὶ Νιόβης, καὶ τὰ μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμόν. κατὰ δὲ Φόρβαντα Ἀκταῖος, ἀφ’ οὗ Ἀκταία ἡ Ἀττική. κατὰ δὲ Τριόπαν Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἄτλας καὶ Ἐπιμηθεὺς καὶ ὁ διφυὴς Κέκροψ καὶ Ἰώ. κατὰ δὲ Κρότωπον ἡ ἐπὶ Φαέθοντος ἐκπύρωσις καὶ ἡ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ἐπομβρία. κατὰ δὲ Σθένελον ἥ τε Ἀμφικτυόνος βασιλεία καὶ ἡ εἰς Πελοπόννησον Δαναοῦ παρουσία καὶ ἡ ὑπὸ Δαρδάνου τῆς Δαρδανίας κτίσις, ὃν πρῶτον, φησὶν Ὅμηρος, τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς, ἥ τε τῆς Εὐρώπης εἰς Κρήτην ἐκ Φοινίκης ἀνακομιδή. κατὰ δὲ Λυγκέα τῆς κόρης ἡ ἁρπαγὴ καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι τεμένους καθίδρυσις Τριπτολέμου τε γεωργία καὶ ἡ Κάδμου εἰς Θήβας παρουσία Μίνωός τε βασιλεία. κατὰ δὲ Προῖτον ὁ Εὐμόλπου πρὸς Ἀθηναίους πόλεμος. κατὰ δὲ Ἀκρίσιον Πέλοπος ἀπὸ Φρυγίας διάβασις καὶ Ἴωνος εἰς Ἀθήνας ἄφιξις καὶ ὁ δεύτερος Κέκροψ αἵ τε Περσέως καὶ Διονύσου πράξεις Ὀρφεύς τε καὶ Μουσαῖος.
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen by the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Now, Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, who was called Plistonices, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he was disposed in a hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by race, and having even composed a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now, this Ptolemaeus was a priest, and in three whole books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their journey out of Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles; and of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the double-born and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations younger, and he is said to be autochthonous as well. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are two generations younger. And from Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are reckoned, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the things of the Assyrians are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt occurred during the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. And in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who was after Inachus, there was the flood of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man; hence, the poet of the Phoroneis says that he was the father of mortal men. From this, Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus; and when he wanted to lead them on to discuss the ancient things, he attempts to speak about the most ancient things of this city, about Phoroneus, who was said to be the first, and about Niobe, and about the things after the flood. And according to Phorbas, Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea comes. And according to Triopas, Prometheus and Atlas and Epimetheus and the double-born Cecrops and Io. And according to Crotopus, the conflagration of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion. And according to Sthenelus, the kingdom of Amphictyon and the arrival of Danaus in Peloponnese and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, and the transportation of Europe from Phoenicia to Crete. And according to Lynceus, the abduction of his daughter and the establishment of the temple in Eleusis, and the agriculture of Triptolemus, and the arrival of Cadmus in Thebes, and the kingdom of Minos. And according to Proetus, the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. And according to Acrisius, the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia and the arrival of Ion in Athens, and the second Cecrops, and the deeds of Perseus and Dionysus, and Orpheus and Musaeus.

pass_b_english: I will discuss shortly the fact that the philosophers' doctrines were borrowed from the Hebrews, but first, as is fitting, I must address the times of Moses. It is through these that the philosophy of the Hebrews will be demonstrated beyond dispute to be the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his work *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical* works. Nevertheless, this memorandum also requires me to run through the points relevant to the present context.

The grammarian Apion, surnamed Plistonices, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History* — though he writes with a hostile disposition toward the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth who even composed a book against the Jews — cites Amosis, the king of Egypt, and the events of his reign. He produces Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's own words run as follows: "Amosis, having become king in the time of the Argive Inachus, razed Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles." This Ptolemy was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books. He states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

Now, the oldest of the Greek traditions are the Argolic — that is, those deriving from Inachus — as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Of these, the Attic traditions, which stem from Cecrops the double-born and autochthonous, are forty generations younger, just as Tatian states verbatim. The Arcadian traditions, which come from Pelasgus, who is also said to be autochthonous, are nine generations younger. The Phthiotic traditions, deriving from Deucalion, are two generations younger still. From Inachus down to the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations, or perhaps a few more, are reckoned — amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years.

If, however, the history of the Assyrians is older than the Greek histories by many years, as Ctesias claims, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian king Amosis and the Argive Inachus will be shown to have occurred in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire and the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belus. Meanwhile, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, the flood of Ogyges took place, and the kingdom in Sicyon began — first under Aegialeus, then Europs, then Telchin — along with the reign of Crete in Crete. Acusilaus declares that Phoroneus was the first man; consequently, the poet of the *Phoroneis* calls him the father of mortal men. Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that, wishing to draw his interlocutors into a discussion of antiquity, he attempts to recount the most ancient traditions of the city, speaking of Phoroneus, who was said to be first, of Niobe, and of the events after the flood.

Under Phorbas came Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea takes its name. Under Triopas came Prometheus, Atlas, Epimetheus, the double-born Cecrops, and Io. Under Crotopus occurred the conflagration of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus fell the reign of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, and the founding of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer calls the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, together with the carrying off of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete. Under Lynceus came the abduction of his daughter, the founding of the sanctuary at Eleusis, the agriculture of Triptolemus, the arrival of Cadmus in Thebes, and the reign of Minos. Under Proetus occurred the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. Under Acrisius came the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia, the arrival of Ion in Athens, the second Cecrops, and the exploits of Perseus and Dionysus, as well as Orpheus and Musaeus.

review.notes: Checked all clauses in paragraph 1. Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Greek text, including the complex genealogical and chronological lists. Scripture citations (Plato, Timaeus; Homer) are correctly handled as literary references. The translation of 'ἐσκευωρῆσθαι' as 'seen by' (A) or 'borrowed from' (B) is a matter of interpretation of the nuance of the Greek, and both are acceptable within the bounds of the text. The translation of 'Βηλούχου' as 'Belus' is correct. All names and historical figures match.
